title: Start with time. The verb stays second.
objective: Place the finite verb in second constituent position after a fronted time phrase.
explanation: In a German declarative main clause, the finite verb is always in the second constituent position — not the second word, but the second constituent. When a time phrase like "Heute" opens the sentence, the verb must still come second and the subject follows it: "Heute arbeite ich zu Hause." This is the same V2 pattern as in Danish. Subordinate clauses and questions follow different rules and should be treated separately.
sourceReference: Teacher-authored example. V2 rule verified against standard German grammar: the finite verb occupies the second syntactic position in a declarative main clause.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly places the finite verb second after a time phrase?
exercises.feedbackCorrect: Correct. "Heute" is the first constituent; "arbeite" is the finite verb in second position; "ich" (subject) follows.
exercises.feedbackIncorrect: The finite verb must come directly after the opening time phrase. The target pattern is "Heute arbeite ich zu Hause."

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "Morgen ___ wir in die Schule."
exercises.feedbackCorrect: Correct. "Morgen" opens the sentence; "gehen" is the finite verb in second position; "wir" follows.
exercises.feedbackIncorrect: After the time phrase "Morgen", the finite verb must come next: "Morgen gehen wir in die Schule."

exercises.prompt: Write a new German sentence that begins with a time phrase (e.g. Heute, Morgen, Am Montag). Then check: is the finite verb in second position?
